newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - U.S. laws strike fear into heart of Mexico.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. laws strike fear into heart of Mexico.

text.p: This farming town was cursed from the start: no mines in a mining state, no oil in a country of oil, not even a railroad.
"We have nothing but the fields," town historian Juan de Santiago Silva told Reuters, "and even they don't want to produce because they're tired."

Emigration is all that has saved Jerez, but now people here see storm clouds overhead. New laws in the United States are cracking down with unprecented force against illegal aliens and curbing benefits for legal migrants.

The toughest new U.S. law came into force on April 1, a day dubbed "Black Tuesday" in Mexico. It authorises hiring of thousands of new border guards, fines immigrants for illegal border crossings and bars deported immigrants from returning for up to 10 years.

The official population of Jerez, about 350 miles (560 km) northwest of Mexico City, is 13,500. But at any one time thousands more are in the United States working legally or illegally and sending home dollars.
The "Black Tuesday" law has created fear for citizens like Maria Marquez, who has three sons and a daughter working in Denver, Colorado, and no other source of income.

"They (her children) just got papers for 10 years and now I hear on the television that all (Mexican immigrants) will have to leave whether they have papers or not," she said, standing in Jerez's central plaza.
"I'm worried," she said. "If my children have to come back, how are they going to support their families? We live off the money they send us."
RESTRICTIONS ON LEGAL IMMIGRANTS

Although legal immigrants will not be deported under the law, it does restrict their rights to such benefits as welfare, said Fernando Robledo Martinez, president of the Centre for Migratory Studies in Zacatecas, capital of the state with the same name where Jerez is a luckless hamlet.
"All of this is going to impact Zacatecas, that is clear," Robledo said. "We just don't know what magnitude yet. It's a real predicament."

Felipe Avila, a security guard in Jerez, said he has an array of cousins, in-laws and friends in California, ticking off a list of cities like a native of the U.S. state. "There have been crises here that we have been able to withstand thanks to our people who live over there and send money," he told Reuters. "Now nobody knows what is going to happen."
A RITE OF SPRING

For many Mexicans, migrating north in search of work is not a criminal act but an annual rite born of economic necessity. Any U.S. attempt to protect its borders, or any mistreatment of Mexican immigrants, raises howls of protest.

Zacatecas state is a leading source of migrants to the United States with seven percent of its 1.3 million people north of the border at any one time and $240 million a year in remittances coming home.

Migratory traditions here run deep, started primarily by tumbling silver prices at the turn of the century, Robledo said. Current migration patterns began during the world wars, which created labour shortages in the United States.

From Jerez, most immigrants gravitate toward Los Angeles, Chicago and San Antonio, Texas, town historian de Santiago Silva said. "You can't knock on a door in this city without finding one of us who has a cousin, an uncle, a friend, a brother ... we all have someone there. It has been an important factor in our economy, unquestionably."
Still, some in Jerez wonder if it might not be so bad if more people stayed home. They complain that "dollar fever" has led many local people to return from the United States with new vices.
Felipe Escobar, 88 years old, the proud son of fighters in the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution and a gadfly fixture at City Hall, said immigration had wounded the national spirit.

"In all of Mexico, people are abandoning the homeland for the cause of the dollar," Escobar told Reuters, brandishing a pistol tucked in the holster beneath his coat. "I would never go there. I'm no fool. Our doom here in Mexico is the dollar."
